steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Describe: state what the data shows using numbers and features (e.g. ‘The median is 45 and the IQR is 12’); do not explain why

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Explain: give reasons for what the data shows (e.g. ‘The median is higher because older participants had more experience’); link to context

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Compare: state similarities and differences between groups, using comparative language and specific data values from each group

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evaluate: weigh up strengths and weaknesses, or assess the usefulness/validity of a method or result; reach a balanced judgement

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: A question asks: ‘Describe the distribution of the data shown in the box plot.’ What should you include in your answer? | Q: A question asks: ‘Compare the heights of the two groups.’ You write: ‘Group A has mean 162 cm and Group B has mean 158 cm.’ Why would this not get full marks? | Q: A question asks you to ‘Evaluate the use of a questionnaire to collect data about diet.’ What two things should your answer include?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: State the median, quartiles, IQR, and range. Mention skewness (e.g. positively skewed if the upper whisker is longer). Give specific values from the box plot. Do not explain why it is skewed. | You must compare both location and spread. Use comparative language (‘Group A is taller on average by 4 cm’) and also compare spread (IQR or SD). State differences explicitly rather than just listing  | Strengths (e.g. cheap, large sample possible, easy to analyse) and weaknesses (e.g. social desirability bias, recall inaccuracy, low response rate). Reach a balanced judgement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Before writing, identify the command word and underline it — it tells you the depth of response required For ‘describe’ questions, use specific data values: quote medians, quartiles, ranges rather than vague terms like ‘bigger’ For ‘compare’ questions, always write about both groups in the same sentence: ‘Group A’s median (32) is higher than Group B’s (28)’ For ‘evaluate’ questions, give both sides before your judgement; one-sided answers lose marks When reading from charts, always check if the axis starts at 0 — a truncated axis can exaggerate differences
